title: A $1 Million Lottery Win, Then an Arrest Days Later
summary:
Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales held an oversized check for $1 million and smiled in a photo posted by the Massachusetts State Lottery.

It was the first puzzle ticket he had ever scratched. He had matched 11 words on a $10 scratch ticket, and local media reported that he planned to save and invest his winnings.

A few days later, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as ICE, said it had arrested him. ICE said officers arrested him on Tuesday, November 24, during operations in East Boston, Massachusetts.

The agency said he will remain in ICE custody until he is removed from the United States. ICE said he entered the United States illegally on May 15, 2013, and that an immigration judge ordered him removed on April 24, 2014.

ICE said the lottery ticket “ultimately led to his arrest,” without explaining how. He does not yet appear on ICE's Online Detainee Locator System, where the public can search for people held in the agency's custody.

It is unclear if he has legal representation. A woman identifying herself as his sister-in-law wrote on Facebook asking for respect and empathy for him, his wife and children. Another woman identifying herself as his older sister wrote that she hoped he would soon be back home with his family.

The Massachusetts State Lottery treats a winner's name, town and prize as public information, and Massachusetts does not let winners claim prizes anonymously. Its website says anyone age 18 and up who is physically present in the state can buy lottery tickets and win prizes.

The Boston Globe reports that the lottery does not require winners to have social security numbers, but that non-resident winners often face higher federal taxes on their winnings.
why_it_matters: The story shows how a public lottery win can draw wide attention, and how immigration rules can shape what happens to a person after a moment of good luck.

background_read: A scratch ticket is a lottery game where players scratch off a coating to see if the hidden words or numbers match a prize.
In Massachusetts, the names, towns and prizes of lottery winners are public information, so a big win can become widely known.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as ICE, is the agency that enforces immigration laws, and it can arrest and hold people it says are in the country without permission.
An immigration judge can order a person to be removed from the country, and people in ICE custody may wait while that process moves forward.
